subject: science
passage: Kestrels, small falcons that hunt voles in open fields, nest in holes in trees and buildings, which are scarce on modern farmland. Ornithologist Petra Nováková placed nest boxes on 30 farms in the Czech Republic early in 2020 and recorded how many were used by kestrels each year, along with the average number of chicks that flew from each used box. She reported that kestrels took several years to adopt the boxes, but that once a box was in use, it produced chicks at a steady rate.

data.title: Kestrel Use of 30 Farm Nest Boxes, 2020–2023

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nováková's report?

choices.A: The number of chicks fledged per used box rose steadily as more boxes came into use.
choices.B: Fewer than a third of the boxes were in use in 2021, the second year of the project.
choices.C: The total number of chicks fledged from all the boxes rose each year from 2020 to 2023.
choices.D: The number of boxes used climbed from 4 in 2020 to 23 in 2023, while chicks fledged per used box stayed near 4 every year.

explanation.why: The report has two parts: adoption was slow (the number of boxes used grew over several years) and output per box was steady. The support must use both columns: boxes used went 4, 9, 17, 23, while chicks per used box stayed between 3.8 and 4.1.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This misreads the table: chicks per used box did not rise steadily; it went 3.9, 4.1, 3.8, 4.0.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (9 of 30), but it describes a single year and says nothing about chicks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but a rising total only reflects more boxes being used; it does not show whether each box produced chicks at a steady rate.
explanation.D: Correct. The rising count of boxes used shows gradual adoption, and the nearly constant chicks per box shows the steady rate, so this supports both parts.
